title: Apple Plans New macOS Full Disk Access Controls for AI-Agent Risks
dek: Apple wants users to better understand the privacy risks before giving applications access to files, mail, messages and browsing history.
metaDescription: Apple plans explicit user action for macOS Full Disk Access, citing AI-agent privacy risks. No implementation date has been announced.

sections.heading: Apple puts explicit consent at the center
sections.body:
Apple has announced plans to introduce additional controls for macOS Full Disk Access, saying that granting the permission will require very explicit user action. The company linked the change to privacy risks associated with AI agents and published its announcement in a post aimed at developers. [1][2][3]

Apple's stated objective is to help users understand those risks before deciding whether to grant access. The emphasis is on an informed decision about data and privacy: users should understand what they are authorizing, rather than give an application broad access without fully appreciating the consequences. [1][2]

The announcement establishes the intended direction, but not a rollout schedule. Apple did not say when the additional controls would be implemented. For now, the confirmed news is a planned change to the process of granting Full Disk Access, with explicit user action as its central requirement. [2][4]

sections.heading: The permission reaches beyond ordinary files
sections.body:
Full Disk Access allows applications to access files, mail, messages and browsing history. According to Apple, it largely bypasses controls designed to protect users' private data. That combination explains the focus on understanding the permission: the decision concerns multiple categories of personal information, not simply access to a single file. [2][3][4]

The permission also has a practical purpose. Full Disk Access allows backup applications to function properly, making those applications an example of why users may need to grant it. Apple's announcement pairs that existing use with a call for more explicit authorization and a clearer understanding of the associated privacy risks. [1][2]

Apple said some developers use Full Disk Access in ways that could expose users' data without their full knowledge and understanding. Its concern therefore includes the gap between granting a permission and understanding how an application may use the resulting access. [1][3]

sections.heading: AI agents widen Apple's privacy concern
sections.body:
Apple said the risks associated with Full Disk Access will grow as AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous. The company's warning connects the scope of the permission with the growing capabilities of the applications receiving it: access to private information is the underlying issue, while agent autonomy adds to Apple's concern. [1][2][3]

The privacy implications also extend beyond the person granting access. Apple said communication applications using Full Disk Access can compromise the privacy of people with whom users communicate. A user's authorization can therefore have implications for others whose information is part of those communications, which makes the consent decision broader than an assessment of the user's own data alone. [2][3][4]

Taken together, these concerns explain Apple's stated preference for informed decisions. Its announcement asks users to understand both the access they grant and the privacy risks associated with that access before proceeding. [1][2]

sections.heading: The announced safeguard is a consent step
sections.body:
The concrete commitment is additional controls requiring very explicit user action before an application receives Full Disk Access. Apple's stated goal is that users understand the risks and make informed choices about their data and privacy. Those are the elements of the announced change, rather than a specified implementation date. [1][2][4]

For developers, the announcement highlights Apple's concern that some uses of the permission may expose data without users' full understanding. For users, the relevant facts are the permission's reach into files, mail, messages and browsing history, alongside its role in helping backup applications work properly. Those facts provide the basis for the decision Apple wants users to make. [1][2][3]

The distinction to retain is between Apple's announced intention and its delivery schedule. The company has committed to additional controls and explicit action, but has not announced when those controls will arrive. [2][4]

keyTakeaways: Apple plans additional macOS Full Disk Access controls requiring very explicit user action. [1][2]
The permission covers files, mail, messages and browsing history, and helps backup applications function properly. [2][3]
Apple says increasingly capable and autonomous AI agents will increase the associated privacy risks. [1][4]
No implementation date has been announced. [2][4]
whyItMatters: Apple's announced approach centers on whether users understand a broad permission before granting it. Because Apple says communication applications can also compromise other people's privacy, the consent decision has implications beyond the person authorizing access. [2][3]
